source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Retirement of experienced nurses, limited nursing-faculty capacity, and workplace burnout or turnover that reduces the available workforce.","B":"A sustained national decline in demand for nursing services because population aging reduces the need for direct clinical care.","C":"An oversupply of nursing faculty and training slots that produces more graduates than healthcare organizations are able to employ.","D":"The absence of identifiable workforce factors, because nursing shortages are primarily random annual fluctuations without persistent causes."}}
source_row.rationale: Recognized contributing factors to ongoing nursing workforce shortages include an aging nursing workforce approaching retirement, nursing faculty shortages that limit nursing school capacity to educate new students, and workplace factors (such as heavy workloads, inadequate staffing, and burnout) contributing to turnover and early exit from the profession.
source_row.source_detail: NCSBN 2026 survey launch summarizes 2024 findings: ~40% intent to leave/retire within five years; stress/burnout, workload and understaffing among leading reasons. AACN July 2026 faculty-shortage data corroborate education-capacity constraints. NCSBN posted 2026-03-24; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15. Reviewed 2026-08-15.
source_row.source_name: National Council of State Boards of Nursing / AACN — Nursing Workforce Shortage Analysis
source_row.stem: A nurse researcher studying the ongoing nursing shortage identifies several contributing factors, and a policy maker assumes the shortage is really just a random yearly fluctuation with no identifiable underlying cause. Which of the following is instead a recognized contributing factor to nursing workforce shortages?
